title: Eight winds
hookLine: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain

cards: People in China tell a story about the poet Su Dongpo. He wrote a poem saying his meditation had grown so steady that the eight winds could not move him, and sent it across the river to his friend, a monk.
The monk wrote one rude word on it and sent it back. The poet, furious, rowed straight over to complain. The monk laughed: eight winds can't move you, but one little puff blew you across the river.
The story is legend. The eight winds are not; they come from a short sutta in the Book of Eights.

teach.b: These eight worldly conditions, the Buddha says, turn the world, and the world turns after them. Gain and loss. Fame and disrepute.
Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. Four pairs: one side we chase, the other we run from, and between the chasing and the running, a lot of life goes by.
In Pali they're the lokadhamma, the ways of the world.
The East Asian name, eight winds, is a good picture: they come and go, they push from different sides, and you don't choose the weather. In the next discourse he makes a sharp point.
These eight come to everyone, to the person who hasn't heard the teaching and to the noble disciple who has.
So what's the difference? The untaught person, when gain comes, doesn't reflect that it's impermanent, painful, bound to change. So gain grabs their mind, and when loss comes, loss grabs it too.
They're delighted, then crushed, and they don't get free.
The taught disciple meets the same eight and sees them for what they are: neither gain nor loss takes over the mind. The disciple still gets praised and still gets blamed.
Practice doesn't stop the weather; it changes how much the weather decides. That's the poet's joke, too. He was right about the eight winds, and wrong about himself.

how: Buddhist teachers in many traditions teach the eight worldly conditions as a check on daily life, and in East Asian Buddhism the 'eight winds' are a common image in sermons and poems about steadiness of mind.

o: four pairs of ups and downs that hit everyone
eight storms that ruined an ancient city
eight breaths that begin a meditation session

s: the sutta says awakened disciples stop meeting praise and blame
the eight come to everyone; the difference is whether they take over the mind.
lokadhamma means 'the ways of the world'
the eight worldly conditions that turn the world.
the story of the poet and the monk is told in the sutta
it's a later Chinese story people tell; the eight conditions come from the sutta.

games.q: both a taught disciple and an untaught person receive the same praise. what's the difference, in the sutta?
o: the disciple sees it as impermanent, and it doesn't take over the mind.
games.why: the wind blows on both. the disciple sees it as impermanent and bound to change, so praise doesn't seize the mind, and blame doesn't either.

practice: Ask which wind blew hardest on you today, gain or loss, praise or blame, pleasure or pain, and name it plainly, the way a forecaster names the weather.
Feel where it lands in the body, then watch it the way you'd watch wind move a tree: it came, it's moving, it will pass, and the tree stays rooted.

wordCard.voice: Eight winds. Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain: the eight worldly conditions that blow through every life. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali lokadhamma: 'world-conditions,' the eight worldly conditions.

carryVoice: Your line: let the wind blow past. Praise and blame still come; they just don't get the last word. Rest well.
